selectedCourses.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
selectedCourses.contribution: Mandatory Year-1 academic writing, scholarly source evaluation, research questions and community-engaged reflection support interdisciplinary learning; not a substitute for a thesis.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Economics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
selectedCourses.contribution: Microeconomic markets, strategic choice and short-run macroeconomic models supply the economic lens on societal and organisational questions.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

selectedCourses.name: Public Economics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
selectedCourses.contribution: Public goods, externalities, taxation, redistribution, welfare and social insurance provide substantive economic analysis of inequality and collective policy choices.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

selectedCourses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
selectedCourses.contribution: Measurement, sampling, design, estimation, hypothesis testing and regression support empirical social/behavioural inquiry through an actual data-collection project.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

selectedCourses.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, emotional expression and suppression, emotional labor, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership and social interaction under conflict, exclusion and interpersonal uncertainty. It emphasises inclusive leadership and ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences, with digital emotion regulation as a further strand. Students conduct a supervised quantitative survey project: formulating theory-driven hypotheses, selecting established psychological measures, designing and piloting a Qualtrics survey, recruiting participants ethically, collecting original data and preparing a clean dataset. Individual work applies descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio, and interprets findings and limitations in empirical reports and evidence-based leadership recommendations.
selectedCourses.contribution: Emotion regulation, belonging, identity safety and inclusive leadership connect minority experiences and social interaction with a supervised quantitative inclusion survey; not general wellbeing or all diversity policy.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership in diverse contexts, with particular attention to minority experiences. Students design and pilot a quantitative survey, collect data ethically, and use SPSS or RStudio for descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression. They interpret the findings and develop evidence-based leadership recommendations.

selectedCourses.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
selectedCourses.contribution: Motivation, teams, power, organisational structure/culture and evidence synthesis provide sustained organisational-behaviour inquiry, not generic leadership alone.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership examines the psychological, social and structural dynamics of organisations. Case discussions and research-based frameworks address motivation, leadership, group dynamics, organisational culture, power, conflict and change.

reusedSharedDescriptionReview.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

selectedCourses.name: AI Ethics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
selectedCourses.contribution: Fairness, privacy, responsibility, agency and psychological human-AI interaction provide substantive digital-ethics inquiry, not programming.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

reusedSharedDescriptionReview.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Data Science
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
selectedCourses.contribution: R-based cleaning, joining, visualization and textual/spatial data analysis support research; no neuroscience-specific dataset or statistical-inference sequence is assumed.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Programming
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
selectedCourses.contribution: Python control flow, functions, recursion, data collections, testing and debugging provide actual algorithmic problem-solving and computational tools.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.

selectedCourses.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
selectedCourses.contribution: Institutions, actors, justice and systemic/technological responses support sustainability transformation; stakeholder inquiry and policy advice give defined applied governance work.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

selectedCourses.name: Climate Change
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
selectedCourses.contribution: Climate mechanisms, impacts, justice, governance and mitigation/adaptation connect physical change to societal responses and communication.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.

selectedCourses.name: Law, Society & Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
selectedCourses.contribution: Legal traditions, public/private law and socio-legal justice questions provide foundational legal/normative inquiry with case reasoning and a research proposal.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.

selectedCourses.name: Modern History
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
selectedCourses.contribution: Political, economic and cultural change since 1815 contextualises democracy, nationalism, imperialism and social transformation; narrower in period than all European history.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

selectedCourses.name: Histories of Gender
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
selectedCourses.contribution: Intersectional North American gender histories, primary sources, queer lives and activism examine how institutions and cultural narratives shape identity and resistance.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.

reusedSharedDescriptionReview.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

selectedCourses.name: Native American Histories
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
selectedCourses.contribution: Indigenous social/cultural histories, institutional violence and contemporary resurgence provide a distinct historical/cultural account of power and collective agency.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Native American Histories studies Indigenous social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, reciprocity and relational accountability guide collaboration with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders through arts-based work and a public-history project.

selectedCourses.name: Researching the “American Century”
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
selectedCourses.contribution: Historical questions, critical source engagement, interdisciplinary thinking and a substantial research paper develop historical inquiry. No archived project, geographic case or detailed period content is assumed beyond the current title and description.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

selectedCourses.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
selectedCourses.contribution: Human-rights law, institutions, landmark cases and philosophical critiques examine rights, dignity, democracy and contested universality.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.

selectedCourses.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines the principles of criminal liability and the legal and moral bases of criminal justice. Students study criminal acts, causation and mental elements, legality, punishment, criminalization, justifications, excuses, inchoate offences and participation. A simulated legal-aid clinic applies doctrine to hypothetical facts through advice memoranda and oral argument. A criminology or organized-crime research proposal develops a literature review and methodology.
selectedCourses.contribution: Criminal liability, punishment, criminalization and justice are tested through legal advice, oral argument and a criminological research proposal.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Public International Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces public international law through its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic legal systems. Legal principles are applied to responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection. The later course examines self-determination, Third World approaches, soft law, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises develop legal reasoning, while a research podcast critically investigates a political dimension of international law.
selectedCourses.contribution: International legal sources, responsibility, force, human rights, self-determination and treaty politics connect law with public power and global institutions.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduction to Public International Law examines its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic law. Topics include responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection, followed by self-determination, Third World approaches, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises and a research podcast develop legal reasoning and critical analysis.

selectedCourses.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.
selectedCourses.contribution: Constitutional structures, rights, judicial review and administrative fairness are studied through concrete cross-system comparison and legal application.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Comparative Constitutional Law compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students study federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review, human rights, public participation and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and hypothetical cases.

selectedCourses.name: Principles of Private Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines property, tort and contract law through comparison of legal systems, primarily Germany, France, England, China and the United States. Students analyze rights and obligations, ownership, nuisance, negligence, contract formation and fairness, remedies and related policy pressures. Legal issue briefs apply the IRAC method. An issue-based comparative contract-law paper and simulated mediation develop comparative analysis, legal argument and negotiation.
selectedCourses.contribution: Comparative property, tort and contract law examines private rights, obligations, policy pressures and negotiated remedies.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines principles of property, tort and contract law and other selected areas of private law. It compares legal systems including Germany, France, England, China and the United States, and considers the social, economic and political pressures underlying legal principles.

reusedSharedDescriptionReview.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

selectedCourses.name: Foundations of European Union Law
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.
selectedCourses.contribution: EU institutions, supremacy, judicial remedies, citizenship and free movement provide substantive regional legal-order inquiry with digital/green applications.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
selectedCourses.contribution: Knowledge, ethics, consciousness, freedom and identity introduce critical philosophical arguments relevant to social, legal and mind questions.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.

selectedCourses.name: Ethics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
selectedCourses.contribution: Historical and contemporary ethical theories, goodness and moral argument supply a normative lens on societal choices, without claiming the complete interdisciplinary Evil subject.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

selectedCourses.name: Philosophy of Mind
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. Later inquiries address machine consciousness, virtual worlds, dreaming, perception, transformative experience and the value of experience. Essays develop independent philosophical interpretations and arguments.
selectedCourses.contribution: Identity, consciousness, mind-body theories, neuropsychological cases and machine consciousness provide a philosophical counterpart to empirical cognition.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.

selectedCourses.name: Philosophy of Emotion
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines what emotions are and how they shape knowledge, decision-making, ethics, social life and politics. Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories are compared with historical, phenomenological and contemporary accounts. Love, fear, grief, moods and political anger provide focused cases, alongside emotions in art and their changing relation to time. Students analyze texts and emotional vignettes and develop an independent philosophical paper or a project combining argument with creative work.
selectedCourses.contribution: Philosophical accounts of emotion, knowledge, decision-making and political anger connect conceptual inquiry with emotional/social experience.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.

selectedCourses.name: Free Will, Time & the Self
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Explores free will and agency in relation to time and the self. Historical Greek and Indian perspectives introduce debates about fatalism, determinism, compatibility and moral responsibility; later topics include scientific challenges, addiction, luck and agency in games. The second part examines the reality and experience of time, physics and temporal asymmetries, then developing research linking time, action and selfhood. Essays require close source analysis and an independent argument.
selectedCourses.contribution: Agency, moral responsibility, determinism, luck, time and selfhood add a defined philosophical inquiry into action; not knowledge-and-power equivalence.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.

selectedCourses.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
selectedCourses.contribution: Comparison of democracy, institutions, parties, polarization and participation uses democracy measurement and a theory-guided empirical memo.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.

selectedCourses.name: Theory of International Relations
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
selectedCourses.contribution: Competing international-relations theories, conflict, colonial relationships and climate politics support geopolitical analysis and researched multilateral negotiation.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Theory of International Relations introduces competing approaches to international relations and geopolitics, including realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism and critical theory. Students apply theories to historical and contemporary cases. A United Nations Security Council simulation develops country-position research, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.

selectedCourses.name: European Union Politics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
selectedCourses.contribution: EU institutions, representation and policymaking combine with empirical analysis of parliamentary amendments, ideology and possible interest-group influence.

An empirical project investigates European Parliament committee amendments, relating MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students plan the research, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.

selectedCourses.name: Peace & Conflict
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
selectedCourses.contribution: Inequality, identity, colonial legacies, humanitarian law and peacebuilding integrate legal/social/political inquiry through a research dossier and policy brief.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Peace & Conflict examines conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies connect to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. An interdisciplinary podcast, policy brief and research dossier develop analysis, while reflection examines how assumptions shape inquiry.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Sociology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
selectedCourses.contribution: Solidarity, identity, stratification, migration and inequality ground sociological analysis of social problems through theories and scholarly evidence.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

selectedCourses.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
selectedCourses.contribution: Qualitative research design, ethics, reflexivity, interviews, ethnography, coding and interpretation implement an actual team inquiry into social experience.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

selectedCourses.name: Modern Sociology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
selectedCourses.contribution: Modern and contemporary sociological theories, Black feminist and decolonial perspectives support theoretically grounded interpretation of social phenomena.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.

selectedCourses.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
selectedCourses.contribution: Social movements and environmental justice are examined through Environmental Justice Atlas cases, feminism, anti-colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

selectedCourses.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
selectedCourses.contribution: Civil society, trust, solidarity, public spheres and decolonial theory frame a research project on a civil organisation, movement or initiative.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial perspectives. Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.

Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.

Students examine animal behaviour, research models, welfare and research ethics, then connect biological rhythms and regulatory behaviour to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based report apply neurobiological concepts.

selectedCourses.name: Psycholinguistics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
selectedCourses.contribution: Language acquisition, production, comprehension and impairments connect neuroscience, psychology and experimental approaches to linguistic capacity.

selectedCourses.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
selectedCourses.contribution: Neural signalling, anatomy, development and psychological processes introduce brain-behaviour relationships and interdisciplinary research-article analysis.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

selectedCourses.name: Social Psychology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
selectedCourses.contribution: Social influence, self, groups, prejudice and prosocial behaviour explain individual-collective interaction; the final project designs rather than conducts empirical research.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.

selectedCourses.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
selectedCourses.contribution: Experimental design and multivariable statistical models support health/behavioural research, with assumption checks, model interpretation and data-analysis reporting.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. R, primarily through R Commander, supports practical exercises; data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions to appropriate models, assumption checks and clear reporting.

selectedCourses.name: Psychopathology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines mental health and psychopathology across the lifespan using a biopsychosocial perspective. Historical views, classification and assessment frame biological, psychological, cultural and social explanations of disorders and treatment. Case-based work applies diagnostic concepts to varied presentations. A structured literature-based essay investigates a focused mental-health question through explicit searching, source selection, evidence appraisal and synthesis, with optional use of PRISMA reporting tools.
selectedCourses.contribution: Biopsychosocial psychopathology, diagnostic cases and explicit literature searching/appraisal deepen mental-health inquiry; no professional clinical qualification is claimed.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.

selectedCourses.name: Medical & Health Psychology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.
selectedCourses.contribution: Health inequalities, stress, prevention, chronic illness and clinical-health formulation connect biological, psychological and social influences on health.

selectedCourses.name: Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Introduces clinical psychological assessment and major psychotherapeutic approaches across the lifespan. Students study ethics, diagnostic systems, test reliability and validity, interviews, personality and cognitive assessment, then psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, systemic and integrative treatments. Training sessions develop introductory administration, scoring and interpretation skills. A psychodiagnostic case report integrates findings and treatment recommendations, while self-monitoring examines developing clinical skills.
selectedCourses.contribution: Psychological assessment, measurement quality, clinical interviews and psychotherapeutic approaches provide introductory diagnostic/clinical study and a case report.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Introduces concepts, methods and ethical issues in clinical psychological assessment and psychotherapy. Students compare approaches to assessment and treatment across age groups and learn to evaluate information critically.

selectedCourses.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
selectedCourses.contribution: Systematic review, effect sizes, fixed/random effects, heterogeneity and publication bias support quantitative evidence synthesis through a small group meta-analysis, not an independent thesis.
selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics introduces systematic reviews and meta-analysis to synthesise results across studies. Students use R to conduct analyses, work with data structures and packages, estimate treatment effects and examine their consistency across studies. Presentations and active research tasks develop evidence-synthesis skills.

selectedCourses.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
selectedCourses.evidenceRead: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. selectedCourses.descriptionRead: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.

selectedCourses.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism

conceptJudgments: Closest materially answers the defining ISS/sustainability substance through introductory/modern/contemporary sociology, qualitative inquiry, foundational/experimental statistics, economics/public redistribution, organisational behaviour and inclusive social interaction, politics/law/ethics, environmental justice, governance, climate and sustainable communication. It exceeds generic breadth or contextual relevance. Seven substitutions follow this prior academic concept; the fall-only capacity conflict is repaired with actual spring inclusion/organisational inquiry, not restored offerings.

CNB materially implements the real brain/behaviour major through a gateway, neurobiology, perception/action, higher cognitive functions, language, lifespan, clinical/health/social psychology and statistical/evidence-synthesis inquiry. Social theory, philosophy, politics, AI ethics and data are complementary interdisciplinary lenses. Current meta-analysis is retained for evidence synthesis, not thesis credit.

LPC materially implements actual law/political/cultural inquiry through a sustained legal sequence, democratic/EU/international politics, rights, philosophy, historical research, rhetoric and media/literature. North American gender/Indigenous/media inquiries have explicit cultural/power substance; no claim that they recreate European political/religious history. Description-only GOSHIST312 receives full consideration as historical inquiry with a substantial paper; no archived Walcheren project or unsupported period content.
progressionFinding: All 72 actual placements pass offered-term and earlier formal-prerequisite checks; each 24 unique/180 EC, four per term, Year-1 PPD. Foundation statistics precede experimental statistics and evidence synthesis under advisory preferences. CNB psycholinguistics occurs in its only covered offering, 2027h1, after Brain & Behavior; Neurobiology concurrently supplies complementary foundations, with no additional hard prerequisite invented. Philosophy of Mind moves to the final spring.

Social psychology, health and youth prevention are specific subjects, not an independent counterpart to the full resilience, happiness and well-being course.
Ethical theory, criminal justice and conflict provide relevant lenses but do not establish the integrated Evil subject as a course purpose.
Philosophical and political inquiry alone does not establish the integrated knowledge/power requirement.
Preserve this genuine approved within-theme elective without inventing a selected subject.
Preserve genuine 30-EC approved mobility/minor choice without assigning a UCR-fit subject.
General methods or advanced coursework do not by themselves establish the required Senior Seminar.

Governance advice and climate communication support transformation but do not establish the required 12-EC Sustainability Think Tank and Governance capstone; governance has its stronger taught-course placement.

alignmentFinding: All 26 external and 54 UCR placements reconsidered. Seventeen positive partial subject relationships; nine meaningful external gaps. Introductory sociology is allocated to the actual named major requirement; social psychology gives a bounded individual/collective relationship. Algorithms use actual Python computational work. Qualitative inquiry maps to methodologies, not Senior Seminar. Statistics maps to two named major courses, not a 30-EC bucket. Current meta-analysis is not an independent thesis; child rhetoric is not the theme capstone. Ethical theory, free will and youth extremism do not become integrated Evil, Knowledge and Power, or generic Happiness subjects. Critical environmental justice and governance address two named required theme subjects. Each identity appears once. Optional independent research 15 EC is additional and unscheduled beside required 12-EC thesis.
